Rusty Toads (Rhinella rubescens) begin their life cycle as small, embryonated eggs deposited in temporary ponds characteristic of the Brazilian Cerrado. This modest initial mass, reflecting the yolk-dependent nutritional strategy of the early larval stages, is typical of bufonids that produce large numbers of small offspring. These tadpoles undergo a period of rapid growth and development within the warm aquatic environment, eventually progressing through larval metamorphosis. At the completion of this morphological transformation, the recently metamorphosed juveniles measure approximately 2.23 centimeters  in total length, a size that marks the transition to a more terrestrial existence. This length at metamorphosis is consistent with allometric patterns observed in congeneric species, where the culmination of the Gosner-stage larval phase results in a predictable body size that is critical for juvenile survival and subsequent recruitment into the adult population.

The time from hatching to sexual maturation appears to be influenced by both thermal conditions and resource availability in the wild, but captive-rearing studies at this stable temperature have provided a clear baseline. Such data are invaluable for comparing the developmental physiology of Rhinella rubescens with other members of the Rhinella genus, revealing differences in the pace of life history that are likely linked to the specific ecological pressures of their respective habitats.

The body size at which females first become reproductively active is closely tied to this growth trajectory. Puberty in females is attained at a snout-vent length of approximately 9.98 centimeters [Lp = approximately 9.98 centimeters], indicating that a substantial proportion of the ultimate growth must be completed before the onset of gonadal activity, a common life-history strategy that prioritizes initial structural development over early reproduction.

This pronounced divergence in adult mass underscores the different selective pressures operating on each sex.
